newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia shouldn't dwell on past - ex-Pol Pot aide.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia shouldn't dwell on past - ex-Pol Pot aide.

text.p: Ieng Sary, foreign minister during the Khmer Rouge "killing fields" reign of terror, said Cambodia should not dwell on its troubled past and rejected calls for an international tribunal to try ailing rebel leader Pol Pot.

"If we keep talking about the past...every Cambodian leader has his own past...then we can never be united and develop our country," said Ieng Sary, who was sentenced in absentia with Pol Pot for his crimes during the 1975-79 Maoist regime.
He was pardoned late last year after he broke away from the guerrillas and promised to work for national reconciliation.

Cambodia is seeing a resurgence of political violence exacerbated by the reported capture of Pol Pot, under whose rule more than a million Cambodians are estimated to have died through torture, execution, disease or hard labour in vast agricultural camps.
If the Cambodian people wanted Pol Pot to be brought before a court, the trial should be held in Cambodia without foreign involvement, Ieng Sary told Reuters.
"It is up to the people. If they say Pol Pot should be tried, then the trial should be in Cambodia, in our country. No outsider should interfere in this," he said.
He was speaking late on Thursday in Pailin, the former headquarters of the now-disintegrating Khmer Rouge in the gem- and timber-rich jungle near Cambodia's western border with Thailand.
He predicted that Pol Pot, who was last seen in public in 1979 and who he said was seriously ill and being given oxygen, may die or mysteriously vanish.
"It is possible that he will mysteriously disappear," he said.
International and Cambodian demands have grown for Pol Pot to be tried for his crimes against humanity.
Cambodia's two prime ministers said on Saturday that Pol Pot had been captured by a breakaway Khmer Rouge faction.
In a rare display of public unity the two premiers sent a letter to the United Nations seeking help in bringing to justice those responsible for crimes committed from 1975-79.
The United States later said it would help Cambodia extradite Pol Pot and asked Canada to consider using a Canadian law against genocide to facilitate the process.
Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk said Pol Pot could be tried in a Cambodian court if an international tribunal could not be arranged.

Ieng Sary, 74, who once trekked alongside Pol Pot through the jungle, now heads the Democratic National United Movement (DNUM) which he founded after breaking away from his former comrades with some 4,000 followers last year.
He said Pol Pot was being held by Ta Mok, the one-legged Khmer Rouge army commander.
"Even though they are in conflict, Ta Mok does not want to kill him or send him to face trial," Ieng Sary said.

He appeared to confirm reports by First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh that Pol Pot slaughtered his defence chief Son Sen and 11 of his family members last month at northern Anlong Veng, then fled his base and was captured by the Ta Mok group.

"I want to tell three truths, one is that Pol Pot ordered to kill Son Sen and his family, two, Pol Pot has been in conflict with Ta Mok and three Pol Pot is badly ill, he is surviving on oxygen," Ieng Sary said.

Ieng Sary also said he doubted that the Khmer Rouge's nominal leader and front man Khieu Samphan would accept an offer of amnesty from the Cambodian authorities and join Ranariddh's royalist FUNCINPEC party.

"Khieu Samphan did not recognise the Phnom Penh government, he has his own provisional government in Anlong Veng, so I don't think he will defect to FUNCINPEC and if he joined (Second Prime Minister) Hun Sen will never accept that deal," Ieng Sary said.
Hun Sen and Ranariddh rule Cambodia in a coalition formed out of necessity after U.N.-sponsored polls in May 1993.
